claim: A nucleocytoplasmic pH oscillation was required for the transcriptional response to carbon starvation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: We determined that a nucleocytoplasmic pH oscillation was required for the transcriptional response to carbon starvation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing pH changes and transcriptional responses during carbon starvation.

claim: The SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex is a key mediator of the transcriptional response to carbon starvation.
source: The SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex is a key mediator of this transcriptional response.
evidence: The manuscript presents data on SWI/SNF function during carbon starvation.

claim: A glutamine-rich low-complexity domain (QLC) in the SNF5 subunit of SWI/SNF, and histidines within this sequence, was required for efficient transcriptional reprogramming.
source: A glutamine-rich low-complexity domain (QLC) in the SNF5 subunit of this complex, and histidines within this sequence, was required for efficient transcriptional reprogramming.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data on SNF5 mutants and their effects on transcription.

claim: The SNF5 QLC mediated pH-dependent recruitment of SWI/SNF to an acidic transcription factor in a reconstituted nucleosome remodeling assay.
source: Furthermore, the SNF5 QLC mediated pH-dependent recruitment of SWI/SNF to an acidic transcription factor in a reconstituted nucleosome remodeling assay.
evidence: The manuscript presents in vitro biochemical assay data showing pH-dependent recruitment.

claim: Protonation of histidines within the SNF5 QLC leads to conformational expansion.
source: Simulations showed that protonation of histidines within the SNF5 QLC leads to conformational expansion, providing a potential biophysical mechanism for regulation of these interactions.
evidence: The manuscript presents computational simulation data showing conformational changes upon histidine protonation.

claim: pH changes are a second messenger for transcriptional reprogramming during carbon starvation.
source: Together, our results indicate that pH changes are a second messenger for transcriptional reprogramming during carbon starvation and that the SNF5 QLC acts as a pH sensor.
evidence: The manuscript presents multiple lines of experimental evidence linking pH changes to transcriptional responses.

claim: The SNF5 QLC acts as a pH sensor.
source: Together, our results indicate that pH changes are a second messenger for transcriptional reprogramming during carbon starvation and that the SNF5 QLC acts as a pH sensor.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing pH-dependent function of the SNF5 QLC.

claim: Intracellular pH (pHi) can vary substantially in both space and time.
source: While early work suggested that pHi was a tightly constrained cellular parameter, more recent technologies have revealed that pHi can vary substantially in both space and time (Llopis et al., 1998; Seksek and Bolard, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Changes in pHi can regulate metabolism, development, proliferation, and cell fate.
source: Moreover, changes in pHi can regulate metabolism (Busa and Nuccitelli, 1984; Young et al., 2010), development (Needham and Needham, 1997), proliferation (Busa and Crowe, 1983), and cell fate (Okamoto, 1994), among other processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Stress-associated intracellular acidification appears to be broadly conserved.
source: Intriguingly, stress-associated intracellular acidification appears to be broadly conserved, suggesting that a drop in pHi is a primordial mechanism to coordinate the general cellular stress response (Drummond et al., 1986; Gores et al., 1989; Munder et al., 2016; O'Sullivan and Condon, 1997; Triandafillou et al., 2020; Yao and Haddad, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work across multiple species.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae is adapted to an acidic external environment (pHe), and optimal growth media is typically at pH 4.0–5.5.
source: The budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae is adapted to an acidic external environment (pHe), and optimal growth media is typically at pH 4.0–5.5.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast growth conditions.

claim: The plasma membrane (Pma1) and vacuolar (Vma1) ATPases maintain near neutral pHi of ~7.8 by pumping protons out of the cell and into the vacuole, respectively.
source: The plasma membrane (Pma1) and vacuolar (Vma1) ATPases maintain near neutral pHi of ~7.8 by pumping protons out of the cell and into the vacuole, respectively (Martínez-Muñoz and Kane, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: When cells are starved for carbon, the Pma1 and Vma1 pumps are inactivated, leading to a rapid acidification of the intracellular space to pH ~6.
source: When cells are starved for carbon, these pumps are inactivated, leading to a rapid acidification of the intracellular space to pH ~6 (Kane, 1995; Orij et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The decrease in intracellular pHi upon carbon starvation is crucial for viability.
source: This decrease in intracellular pHi is crucial for viability upon carbon starvation and is thought to conserve energy, leading to storage of metabolic enzymes in filamentous assemblies (Petrovska et al., 2014), reduction of macromolecular diffusion (Joyner et al., 2016; Munder et al., 2016), decreased membrane biogenesis (Young et al., 2010), and possibly the noncovalent crosslinking of the cytoplasm into a solid-like material state (Joyner et al., 2016; Munder et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Transient acidification is required for induction of the transcriptional heat-shock response in some conditions.
source: Recently, evidence was presented of a positive role for acidic pHi in stress-gene induction: transient acidification is required for induction of the transcriptional heat-shock response in some conditions (Triandafillou et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: The Sucrose Non-Fermenting genes (SNF) were among the first genes found to be required for induction of glucose-repressed genes.
source: The Sucrose Non-Fermenting genes (SNF) were among the first genes found to be required for induction of glucose-repressed genes (Neigeborn and Carlson, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Several SNF genes were identified as members of the SWI/SNF complex.
source: Several of these genes were later identified as members of the SWI/SNF complex (Abrams et al., 1986; Carlson, 1987), an 11-subunit chromatin remodeling complex that is highly conserved from yeast to mammals (Chiba et al., 1994; Peterson et al., 1994; Peterson and Herskowitz, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The SWI/SNF complex is highly conserved from yeast to mammals.
source: Several of these genes were later identified as members of the SWI/SNF complex (Abrams et al., 1986; Carlson, 1987), an 11-subunit chromatin remodeling complex that is highly conserved from yeast to mammals (Chiba et al., 1994; Peterson et al., 1994; Peterson and Herskowitz, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The SWI/SNF complex affects the expression of ~10% of the genes in S. cerevisiae during vegetative growth.
source: The SWI/SNF complex affects the expression of ~10% of the genes in S. cerevisiae during vegetative growth (Sudarsanam et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Upon carbon starvation, most genes are downregulated, but a set of glucose-repressed genes, required for utilization of alternative energy sources, are strongly induced.
source: Upon carbon starvation, most genes are downregulated, but a set of glucose-repressed genes, required for utilization of alternative energy sources, are strongly induced (Zid and O'Shea, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: The SWI/SNF complex is required for the efficient expression of several hundred stress-response and glucose-repressed genes.
source: The SWI/SNF complex is required for the efficient expression of several hundred stress-response and glucose-repressed genes, implying a possible function in pH-associated gene expression (Biddick et al., 2008a; Sudarsanam et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: 10/11 subunits of the SWI/SNF complex contain large intrinsically disordered regions.
source: 10/11 subunits of the SWI/SNF complex contain large intrinsically disordered regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and in particular, 4/11 SWI/SNF subunits contain glutamine-rich low-complexity sequences (QLCs).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 4/11 SWI/SNF subunits contain glutamine-rich low-complexity sequences (QLCs).
source: 10/11 subunits of the SWI/SNF complex contain large intrinsically disordered regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and in particular, 4/11 SWI/SNF subunits contain glutamine-rich low-complexity sequences (QLCs).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: QLCs are present in glutamine-rich transactivation domains.
source: QLCs are present in glutamine-rich transactivation domains (Kadonaga et al., 1988; Kadonaga et al., 1987) some of which, including those found within SWI/SNF, may bind to transcription factors (Prochasson et al., 2003) or recruit transcriptional machinery (Geng et al., 2001; Janody et al., 2001; Laurent et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Some QLCs, including those found within SWI/SNF, may bind to transcription factors.
source: QLCs are present in glutamine-rich transactivation domains (Kadonaga et al., 1988; Kadonaga et al., 1987) some of which, including those found within SWI/SNF, may bind to transcription factors (Prochasson et al., 2003) or recruit transcriptional machinery (Geng et al., 2001; Janody et al., 2001; Laurent et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Some QLCs may recruit transcriptional machinery.
source: QLCs are present in glutamine-rich transactivation domains (Kadonaga et al., 1988; Kadonaga et al., 1987) some of which, including those found within SWI/SNF, may bind to transcription factors (Prochasson et al., 2003) or recruit transcriptional machinery (Geng et al., 2001; Janody et al., 2001; Laurent et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Intrinsically disordered regions lack a fixed three-dimensional structure and can be highly responsive to their solution environment.
source: Intrinsically disordered regions lack a fixed three-dimensional structure and can be highly responsive to their solution environment (Holehouse and Sukenik, 2020; Moses et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The SWI/SNF QLCs contain multiple histidine residues.
source: Moreover, the SWI/SNF QLCs contain multiple histidine residues.
evidence: This is a direct observation from sequence analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The intrinsic pKa of the histidine sidechain is 6.9.
source: Given that the intrinsic pKa of the histidine sidechain is 6.9 (Whitten et al., 2005), we hypothesized that these glutamine-rich low-complexity regions might function as pH sensors in response to variations in pHi.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: SNF5 is over 50% disordered.
source: SNF5 is over 50% disordered and contains the largest QLC of the SWI/SNF complex.
evidence: This is based on disorder prediction analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: SNF5 contains the largest QLC of the SWI/SNF complex.
source: SNF5 is over 50% disordered and contains the largest QLC of the SWI/SNF complex.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The SNF5 QLC is 42% glutamine and contains seven histidine residues.
source: This region is 42% glutamine and contains seven histidine residues.
evidence: This is a direct observation from sequence analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Intracellular pH (pHi) is highly dynamic and varies between subpopulations of cells within the same culture.
source: By single-cell analysis, we found that intracellular pH (pHi) is highly dynamic and varies between subpopulations of cells within the same culture.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: After an initial decrease to pHi ~ 6.5 upon carbon starvation, a subset of cells recovered their pHi to ~7.
source: After an initial decrease to pHi ~ 6.5, a subset of cells recovered their pHi to ~7.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Transient acidification followed by recovery was required for expression of glucose-repressed genes.
source: This transient acidification followed by recovery was required for expression of glucose-repressed genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing gene expression under different pH conditions.

claim: The SNF5 QLC and four embedded histidines were required for rapid gene induction.
source: The SNF5 QLC and four embedded histidines were required for rapid gene induction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing wild-type and mutant strains.

claim: SWI/SNF complex histone remodeling activity was robust to pH changes.
source: SWI/SNF complex histone remodeling activity was robust to pH changes, but recruitment of the complex to a model transcription factor was pH-sensitive, and this recruitment was mediated by the SNF5 QLC and histidines within.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro biochemical assay data.

claim: Recruitment of the SWI/SNF complex to a model transcription factor was pH-sensitive.
source: SWI/SNF complex histone remodeling activity was robust to pH changes, but recruitment of the complex to a model transcription factor was pH-sensitive, and this recruitment was mediated by the SNF5 QLC and histidines within.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro biochemical assay data.

claim: Recruitment of SWI/SNF to a model transcription factor was mediated by the SNF5 QLC and histidines within.
source: SWI/SNF complex histone remodeling activity was robust to pH changes, but recruitment of the complex to a model transcription factor was pH-sensitive, and this recruitment was mediated by the SNF5 QLC and histidines within.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro biochemical assay data comparing wild-type and mutant complexes.

claim: All-atom simulations indicated that histidine protonation causes a conformational expansion of the SNF5 QLC.
source: All-atom simulations indicated that histidine protonation causes a conformational expansion of the SNF5 QLC, perhaps enabling interaction with a different set of transcription factors and driving recruitment to the promoters of glucose-repressed genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational simulation data.

claim: Proline and histidine were enriched (>50–100%-fold higher than average proteome abundance) in yeast QLCs.
source: We found that proline and histidine were enriched (>50–100%-fold higher than average proteome abundance) in yeast QLCs (Figure 1B), with similar patterns found in Dictyostelium discoideum, and Drosophila melanogaster proteomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of proteomes presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Similar patterns of proline and histidine enrichment in QLCs were found in Dictyostelium discoideum and Drosophila melanogaster proteomes.
source: We found that proline and histidine were enriched (>50–100%-fold higher than average proteome abundance) in yeast QLCs (Figure 1B), with similar patterns found in Dictyostelium discoideum, and Drosophila melanogaster proteomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of proteomes presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Enrichment for histidine within QLCs was previously described across many Eukaryotes.
source: Enrichment for histidine within QLCs was previously described across many Eukaryotes using a slightly different method (Ramazzotti et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: The codons for glutamine are a single base pair mutation away from proline and histidine.
source: Interestingly, the codons for glutamine are a single base pair mutation away from proline and histidine.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the genetic code.

claim: Histidines are 50% more abundant in yeast QLCs than in all other low-complexity sequences identified using Wootton–Federhen complexity.
source: In fact, this is not the case: histidines are 50% more abundant in yeast QLCs than in all other low-complexity sequences identified using Wootton–Federhen complexity (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The N-terminus of SNF5 contains one of the largest QLCs in the yeast proteome.
source: The N-terminus of SNF5 contains one of the largest QLCs in the yeast proteome and is in the top 3 QLCs in terms of number of histidines (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and F.

claim: The N-terminus of SNF5 is in the top 3 QLCs in terms of number of histidines.
source: The N-terminus of SNF5 contains one of the largest QLCs in the yeast proteome and is in the top 3 QLCs in terms of number of histidines (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and F.

claim: Every Snf5 N-terminal region from 20 orthologous proteins from Ascomycota consisted of at least 18% glutamine (max 43%) and all possessed multiple histidine residues.
source: Despite the relatively poor sequence conservation across the N-terminal disordered regions in SNF5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A), every region consisted of at least 18% glutamine (max 43%) and all possessed multiple histidine residues (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B, Supplementary file 2; the phylogeny considered and the total number of QLCs for each species are shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The SNF5 QLC was likely gained in the lineage leading to the Ascomycota and is not present in most Metazoa (animals).
source: A broader survey of the tree of life (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) indicates that the SNF5 QLC was likely gained in the lineage leading to the Ascomycota and is not present in most Metazoa (animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: snf5Δ strains grew slowly.
source: As previously reported (Laurent et al., 1990), snf5Δ strains grew slowly (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A and a citation to prior work.

claim: Growth rates of ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 were similar to WT during continuous growth in either fermentable (glucose) or poor (galactose or galactose/ethanol) carbon sources.
source: In contrast, growth rates of ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 were similar to WT during continuous growth in either fermentable (glucose) or poor (galactose or galactose/ethanol) carbon sources (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A–D) and showed minimal defects when grown in glucose, carbon-starved for 24 hr, and then reinoculated into glucose media.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A–D.

claim: A strong growth defect was revealed for ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 strains when cells were carbon-starved for 24 hr and then switched to a poor carbon source.
source: However, a strong growth defect was revealed for ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 strains when cells were carbon-starved for 24 hr and then switched to a poor carbon source (Figure 1—figure supplement 6E and F), suggesting that the SNF5 QLC is important for adaptation to new carbon sources.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 6E and F.

claim: Deletion of the SNF5 gene has been shown to disrupt the architecture of the SWI/SNF complex, leading to loss of other subunits.
source: Deletion of the SNF5 gene has been shown to disrupt the architecture of the SWI/SNF complex, leading to loss of other subunits (Peterson et al., 1994; Yang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The entire SWI/SNF complex remained intact in both the ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 strains.
source: We found that the entire SWI/SNF complex remained intact in both the ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 7A.

claim: All SNF5 alleles were expressed at similar levels to wild-type both in glucose and upon carbon starvation.
source: Silver stains of the untagged Snf5p and Western blotting of TAP-tagged SNF5 (Puig et al., 2001) strains showed that all SNF5 alleles were expressed at similar levels to wild-type both in glucose and upon carbon starvation (Figure 1—figure supplement 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 7B.

claim: Deletion of the SNF5 QLC is distinct from total loss of the SNF5 gene.
source: Together, these results show that deletion of the SNF5 QLC is distinct from total loss of the SNF5 gene and that this N-terminal sequence is important for efficient recovery from carbon starvation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different phenotypes observed for ΔQsnf5 and snf5Δ strains.

claim: The N-terminal sequence of SNF5 is important for efficient recovery from carbon starvation.
source: Together, these results show that deletion of the SNF5 QLC is distinct from total loss of the SNF5 gene and that this N-terminal sequence is important for efficient recovery from carbon starvation.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data showing defects in recovery from starvation.

claim: The alcohol dehydrogenase ADH2 gene is normally repressed in the presence of glucose and strongly induced upon carbon starvation.
source: The alcohol dehydrogenase ADH2 gene is normally repressed in the presence of glucose and strongly induced upon carbon starvation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ADH2 regulation.

claim: ADH2 regulation depends on SWI/SNF activity.
source: This regulation depends on SWI/SNF activity (Peterson and Herskowitz, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: The wild-type SWI/SNF complex is robustly recruited to the ADH2 promoter upon carbon starvation.
source: These experiments showed that the wild-type complex is robustly recruited to the ADH2 promoter upon carbon starvation (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: Recruitment of SWI/SNF to the ADH2 promoter is reduced in ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 strains.
source: However, this recruitment is reduced in ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: Robust ADH2 expression after acute carbon starvation was dependent on the SNF5 QLC and the histidines within.
source: We found that robust ADH2 expression after acute carbon starvation was dependent on the SNF5 QLC and the histidines within (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: snf5Δ strains did not completely repress ADH2 expression in glucose and showed partial induction upon carbon starvation.
source: This defect was far stronger in the ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 strains than in snf5Δ strains; snf5Δ strains did not completely repress ADH2 expression in glucose and showed partial induction upon carbon starvation, while ΔQsnf5 strains tightly repressed ADH2 in glucose (similar to WT), but completely failed to induce expression upon starvation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: ΔQsnf5 strains tightly repressed ADH2 in glucose (similar to WT), but completely failed to induce expression upon starvation.
source: This defect was far stronger in the ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 strains than in snf5Δ strains; snf5Δ strains did not completely repress ADH2 expression in glucose and showed partial induction upon carbon starvation, while ΔQsnf5 strains tightly repressed ADH2 in glucose (similar to WT), but completely failed to induce expression upon starvation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: SNF5 has a dual role in ADH2 regulation, both contributing to strong repression in glucose and robust induction upon carbon starvation.
source: These results suggest a dual role for SNF5 in ADH2 regulation, both contributing to strong repression in glucose and robust induction upon carbon starvation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different phenotypes of SNF5 mutants.

claim: After 6 hr of glucose starvation, PADH2-mCherry expression was bimodal in WT strains; about half of the cells had high mCherry fluorescence and half were low.
source: We found high cell-to-cell variation in the expression of this reporter in WT strains: after 6 hr of glucose starvation, PADH2-mCherry expression was bimodal; about half of the cells had high mCherry fluorescence and half were low.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: The bimodality of PADH2-mCherry expression was strongly dependent on preculture conditions.
source: This bimodality was strongly dependent on preculture conditions and was most apparent upon acute withdrawal of carbon from early log-phase cells that had grown for >16 hr with optical density at 600 nm (O.D.) never exceeding 0.3 (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: Complete deletion of SNF5 eliminated the bimodal expression pattern of PADH2-mCherry.
source: Complete deletion of SNF5 eliminated this bimodal expression pattern; again, low levels of expression were apparent in glucose and induction during starvation was attenuated.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: The ΔQsnf5 strain completely failed to induce the PADH2-mCherry reporter at 6 hr after carbon starvation.
source: As in the RT-qPCR analysis, the ΔQsnf5 strain completely failed to induce the PADH2-mCherry reporter at this time point and mutation of four central histidines to alanine was sufficient to mostly abrogate expression (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: Mutation of four central histidines to alanine was sufficient to mostly abrogate PADH2-mCherry expression.
source: As in the RT-qPCR analysis, the ΔQsnf5 strain completely failed to induce the PADH2-mCherry reporter at this time point and mutation of four central histidines to alanine was sufficient to mostly abrogate expression (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: Mutation of a further two histidines (6/7 total) had little additional effect on PADH2-mCherry expression.
source: Mutation of a further two histidines had little additional effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 9B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 9B–D.

claim: The dual function of SNF5 leads to switch-like control of ADH2 expression.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the dual function of SNF5 leads to switch-like control of ADH2 expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed expression patterns.

claim: In glucose, SNF5 helps repress ADH2.
source: In glucose, SNF5 helps repress ADH2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression data showing tight repression in ΔQsnf5 strains.

claim: Upon carbon starvation, SNF5 is required for efficient induction of ADH2.
source: Upon carbon starvation, SNF5 is required for efficient induction of ADH2.
evidence: This claim is supported by expression data showing failure to induce in SNF5 mutants.

claim: The SNF5 QLC and histidine residues within seem to be crucial for switching between repression and induction states of ADH2.
source: The SNF5 QLC and histidine residues within seem to be crucial for switching between these states.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutant phenotypes.

claim: Multiple stresses, including glucose starvation, have been shown to cause a decrease in the pH of the cytoplasm and nucleus (nucleocytoplasm).
source: Multiple stresses, including glucose starvation, have been shown to cause a decrease in the pH of the cytoplasm and nucleus (nucleocytoplasm) (Dechant et al., 2014; Gores et al., 1989; Triandafillou et al., 2020; Yao and Haddad, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Wild-type cells growing exponentially in 2% glucose had a pHi of ~7.8.
source: Wild-type cells growing exponentially in 2% glucose had a pHi of ~7.8.
evidence: This claim is supported by pHluorin measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Upon acute carbon starvation, cells rapidly acidified to pHi ~ 6.5.
source: Upon acute carbon starvation, cells rapidly acidified to pHi ~ 6.5.
evidence: This claim is supported by pHluorin measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: During the first hour of carbon starvation, two populations arose: an acidic population (pHi ~ 5.5), and a second population that recovered to pHi ~ 7.
source: Then, during the first hour, two populations arose: an acidic population (pHi ~ 5.5), and a second population that recovered to pHi ~ 7 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Cells at pHi 7 proceeded to strongly induce expression of the PADH2-mCherry reporter, while cells at pHi 5.5 did not.
source: Cells at pHi 7 proceeded to strongly induce expression of the PADH2-mCherry reporter, while cells at pHi 5.5 did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Cells that neither recovered neutral pH nor expressed the PADH2-mCherry reporter had lower fitness relative to the PADH2-mCherry-inducing population.
source: We used fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) to separate these two populations and found that cells that neither recovered neutral pH nor expressed the PADH2-mCherry reporter had lower fitness relative to the PADH2-mCherry-inducing population, as indicated by lower rates of proliferation on both rich and poor carbon sources, and lower tolerance of heat stress (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth and viability assays presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: After 8 hr of glucose starvation, >70% of wild-type cells had induced ADH2.
source: After 8 hr of glucose starvation, >70% of wild-type cells had induced ADH2 (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2A and C.

claim: ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 strains rapidly acidified upon carbon starvation, similarly to WT.
source: Similarly to WT, both ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 strains rapidly acidified upon carbon starvation.
evidence: This claim is supported by pHluorin measurements presented in Figure 2A.

claim: ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 strains were defective in subsequent neutralization of pHi and in the expression of PADH2-mCherry.
source: However, these strains were defective in subsequent neutralization of pHi and in the expression of PADH2-mCherry.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: At the 4 hr time point after carbon starvation, >95% of both ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 cells remained acidic with no detectable expression, while >60% of wild-type cells had neutralized and expressed mCherry.
source: At the 4 hr time point, >95% of both ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 cells remained acidic with no detectable expression, while >60% of wild-type cells had neutralized and expressed mCherry (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2A and C.

claim: After 24 hr, the majority of ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 mutant cells neutralized to pHi ~7 and induced expression of PADH2-mCherry.
source: Eventually, after 24 hr, the majority of mutant cells neutralized to pHi ~7 and induced expression of PADH2-mCherry (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Complete deletion of SNF5 led to less severe phenotypes than the ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 alleles with only a modest delay in PADH2-mCherry expression.
source: Again, complete deletion of SNF5 led to less severe phenotypes than the ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 alleles with only a modest delay in PADH2-mCherry expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), suggesting that SNF5 plays both activating and inhibitory roles in ADH2 expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The SNF5 QLC and histidines within are required for the rapid dynamics of both transient acidification and transcriptional induction of PADH2-mCherry upon acute carbon starvation.
source: Thus, the SNF5 QLC and histidines within are required for the rapid dynamics of both transient acidification and transcriptional induction of PADH2-mCherry upon acute carbon starvation.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data presented.

claim: New gene expression is required for recovery of pHi after carbon starvation.
source: In these conditions, we found that cells experienced a drop in pHi but were unable to recover neutral pH (Figure 2—figure supplement 5). Thus, new gene expression is required for recovery of pHi.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments with cycloheximide presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The acidification of the yeast nucleocytoplasm has been shown to depend upon an acidic extracellular pH (pHe).
source: The acidification of the yeast nucleocytoplasm has been shown to depend upon an acidic extracellular pH (pHe).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited in the manuscript.

claim: Cell viability was strongly dependent on pHe, decreasing drastically when cells were starved for glucose in media at pH ≥ 7.0 for 24 hr.
source: Cell viability was strongly dependent on pHe, decreasing drastically when cells were starved for glucose in media at pH ≥ 7.0 for 24 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by viability assay data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of PADH2-mCherry expression was highly dependent on pHe, especially in SNF5 QLC mutants.
source: Expression of PADH2-mCherry expression was also highly dependent on pHe, especially in SNF5 QLC mutants (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: WT cells failed to induce PADH2-mCherry at pHe ≥ 7, but induced strongly at pHe ≤ 6.5.
source: WT cells failed to induce PADH2-mCherry at pHe ≥ 7, but induced strongly at pHe ≤ 6.5.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: RT-qPCR showed similar pHe-dependent behavior for the endogenous ADH2 transcript.
source: RT-qPCR showed similar behavior for the endogenous ADH2 transcript (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Recruitment of SWI/SNF to the ADH2 promoter was reduced when starvation was performed with media buffered to pHe 7.5.
source: ChIP experiments indicated that recruitment of SWI/SNF to the ADH2 promoter was also reduced when starvation was performed with media buffered to pHe 7.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: The nucleocytoplasm of all strains failed to acidify when the environment was held at pHe ≥ 7.
source: Furthermore, we found that the nucleocytoplasm of all strains failed to acidify when the environment was held at pHe ≥ 7 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by pHluorin measurements presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: An acidic extracellular environment is required for a decrease in intracellular pH upon carbon starvation.
source: Therefore, we conclude that an acidic extracellular environment is required for a decrease in intracellular pH upon carbon starvation, and that this intracellular acidification is required for activation of ADH2 transcription.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Intracellular acidification is required for activation of ADH2 transcription.
source: Therefore, we conclude that an acidic extracellular environment is required for a decrease in intracellular pH upon carbon starvation, and that this intracellular acidification is required for activation of ADH2 transcription.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Cells treated with sorbic acid to allow intracellular acidification but prevent pHi recovery failed to induce PADH2-mCherry.
source: First, we used the membrane-permeable sorbic acid to allow intracellular acidification but prevent pHi recovery. These cells failed to induce PADH2-mCherry, indicating that nucleocytoplasmic acidification is not sufficient; subsequent neutralization is also required.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Nucleocytoplasmic acidification is not sufficient for PADH2-mCherry induction; subsequent neutralization is also required.
source: First, we used the membrane-permeable sorbic acid to allow intracellular acidification but prevent pHi recovery. These cells failed to induce PADH2-mCherry, indicating that nucleocytoplasmic acidification is not sufficient; subsequent neutralization is also required.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sorbic acid experiment.

claim: Carbon starvation at pHe 7.4 prevented transient acidification and prevented PADH2-mCherry expression.
source: Carbon starvation at pHe 7.4 prevented transient acidification and likewise prevented expression (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cells that were first held at pHe 7.4, preventing initial acidification, and then switched to pHe 5, thereby causing late acidification, failed to express mCherry after 6 hr.
source: Cells that were first held at pHe 7.4, preventing initial acidification, and then switched to pHe 5, thereby causing late acidification, failed to express mCherry after 6 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Starvation at pHe 5 for 2 hr followed by a switch to pHe 7.4, with a corresponding increase in pHi, led to robust PADH2-mCherry expression.
source: Finally, starvation at pHe 5 for 2 hr followed by a switch to pHe 7.4, with a corresponding increase in pHi, led to robust PADH2-mCherry expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Transient acidification immediately upon switching to carbon starvation followed by recovery to neutral pHi is the signal for the efficient induction of PADH2-mCherry.
source: Together, these results suggest that transient acidification immediately upon switching to carbon starvation followed by recovery to neutral pHi is the signal for the efficient induction of PADH2-mCherry.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pH manipulation experiments.

claim: Forcing ΔQsnf5 cells to neutralize pHi does not rescue ADH2 expression.
source: We therefore wondered if forcing cells to neutralize pHi would rescue ADH2 expression in a ΔQsnf5 strain. This was not the case: the ΔQsnf5 strain still fails to express PADH2-mCherry, even if we recapitulate normal intracellular transient acidification (Figure 3B, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: The SNF5 QLC is required for normal kinetics of transient acidification and for additional steps in ADH2 gene activation.
source: Therefore, the SNF5 QLC is required for normal kinetics of transient acidification and for additional steps in ADH2 gene activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Mutation of the QLC of SNF5 does not strongly affect gene expression in rich media.
source: Principal component analysis showed tight clustering of all exponentially growing samples, indicating that mutation of the QLC of SNF5 does not strongly affect gene expression in rich media (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: There are greater differences between wild-type strains with mutant SNF5 alleles upon glucose starvation.
source: In contrast, there are greater differences between wild-type strains with mutant SNF5 alleles upon glucose starvation.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: The genes that accounted for most variation in RNA-seq (the first two principal components) were involved in carbon transport, metabolism, and stress responses.
source: The genes that accounted for most variation (the first two principal components) were involved in carbon transport, metabolism, and stress responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: 89 genes were induced (greater than threefold) and 60 genes were downregulated (greater than threefold) in WT strains upon starvation in media titrated to pHe 5.
source: We defined a set of 89 genes that were induced (greater than threefold) and 60 genes that were downregulated (greater than threefold) in WT strains upon starvation in media titrated to pHe 5.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Many genes induced in WT upon starvation were poorly induced in ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 mutants, as well as in WT strains starved in media titrated to suboptimal pHe 7.
source: Many of these genes were poorly induced in ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 mutants, as well as in WT strains starved in media titrated to suboptimal pHe 7 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Group 1 genes (n = 42) were activated in starvation in an SNF5 QLC and pH-dependent manner.
source: Group 1 genes (n = 42) were activated in starvation in an SNF5 QLC and pH-dependent manner. They are strongly induced in WT, but induction is attenuated both in mutants of the SNF5 QLC and when the transient acidification of pHi was prevented by starving cells in media titrated to pHe 7.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and hierarchical clustering analysis presented in Figure 4E.

claim: Group 1 genes are enriched for processes that are adaptive in carbon starvation, for example, fatty acid metabolism and the TCA cycle.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis revealed that these genes are enriched for processes that are adaptive in carbon starvation, for example, fatty acid metabolism and the TCA cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Group 2 (n = 64) genes were not strongly induced in WT, but were inappropriately induced during starvation in SNF5 QLC mutants and during starvation at pHe 7.
source: Group 2 (n = 64) genes were not strongly induced in WT, but were inappropriately induced during starvation in SNF5 QLC mutants and during starvation at pHe 7.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and hierarchical clustering analysis presented in Figure 4E.

claim: Group 2 genes are enriched for stress responses.
source: GO analysis revealed that these genes are enriched for stress responses, perhaps because the failure to properly reprogram transcription leads to cellular stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Group 3 genes (n = 51) were repressed upon carbon starvation in a pH-dependent but SNF5 QLC-independent manner.
source: Group 3 genes (n = 51) were repressed upon carbon starvation in a pH-dependent but SNF5 QLC-independent manner. They were repressed in all strains, but repression failed at pHe 7.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and hierarchical clustering analysis presented in Figure 4E.

claim: Group 4 genes (n = 16) were repressed in WT cells in a pH-independent manner, but failed to repress in SNF5 QLC mutants.
source: Finally, group 4 genes (n = 16) were repressed in WT cells in a pH-independent manner, but failed to repress in SNF5 QLC mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and hierarchical clustering analysis presented in Figure 4E.

claim: Top transcription factor hits for group 1 genes included the CAT8 and ADR1 transcription factors.
source: Top hits for group 1 included the CAT8 and ADR1 transcription factors, which have previously been suggested to recruit the SWI/SNF complex to the ADH2 promoter (Biddick et al., 2008b).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcription factor enrichment analysis and a citation to prior work.

claim: CAT8 and ADR1 transcription factors have previously been suggested to recruit the SWI/SNF complex to the ADH2 promoter.
source: Top hits for group 1 included the CAT8 and ADR1 transcription factors, which have previously been suggested to recruit the SWI/SNF complex to the ADH2 promoter (Biddick et al., 2008b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Both pH changes and the SNF5 QLC are required for correct transcriptional reprogramming upon carbon starvation.
source: In conclusion, both pH changes and the SNF5 QLC are required for correct transcriptional reprogramming upon carbon starvation, but the dependencies are nuanced.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the RNA-seq data.

claim: A set of genes, including many of the traditionally defined 'glucose-repressed genes,' require both the SNF5 QLC and a pH change for their induction upon carbon starvation (group 1).
source: Finally, a set of genes, including many of the traditionally defined 'glucose-repressed genes,' require both the SNF5 QLC and a pH change for their induction upon carbon starvation (group 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: For group 1 genes, point mutation of four histidines in the QLC is almost as perturbative as complete deletion of the QLC.
source: For these genes, point mutation of four histidines in the QLC is almost as perturbative as complete deletion of the QLC.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data comparing ΔQsnf5 and HtoAsnf5 strains.

claim: Group 1 genes are enriched for genes involved in catabolism, TCA cycle, and metabolism.
source: It is striking that this set is enriched for genes involved in catabolism, TCA cycle, and metabolism, given that these processes are important for energetic adaptation to acute glucose starvation.
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Recent structural evidence shows that the QLCs of not only SNF5 but also several other SWI/SNF subunits appear to be poised for interaction with transcription factors on DNA immediately downstream of the nucleosome.
source: Indeed, recent structural evidence (He et al., 2021) shows that the QLCs of not only SNF5 but also several other SWI/SNF subunits appear to be poised for interaction with transcription factors on DNA immediately downstream of the nucleosome (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work and structural analysis presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: SWI/SNF complexes containing either ΔQsnf5p or HtoAsnf5 retained full nucleosome remodeling activity.
source: In this assay, SWI/SNF complexes containing either ΔQsnf5p or HtoAsnf5 retained full nucleosome remodeling activity (Figure 5B–D), as well as full DNA-stimulated ATPase activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro FRET-based remodeling assay data presented in Figure 5B–D.

claim: SWI/SNF complexes containing either ΔQsnf5p or HtoAsnf5 retained full DNA-stimulated ATPase activity.
source: In this assay, SWI/SNF complexes containing either ΔQsnf5p or HtoAsnf5 retained full nucleosome remodeling activity (Figure 5B–D), as well as full DNA-stimulated ATPase activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATPase assay data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The nucleosome remodeling and ATPase activities of SWI/SNF were similar at pH 6.5, 7, or 7.6.
source: Furthermore, these activities were similar at pH 6.5, 7, or 7.6.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro assay data at different pH values.

claim: The SNF5 QLC does not sense pH by modifying its intrinsic ATPase and nucleosome remodeling activity, at least in this in vitro context.
source: Thus, we conclude that the SNF5 QLC does not sense pH by modifying its intrinsic ATPase and nucleosome remodeling activity, at least in this in vitro context.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vitro assay data.

claim: The QLC of Snf5p mediates interaction with the Gal4-VP16 transcription factor.
source: Indeed, it was previously demonstrated that the QLC of Snf5p mediates interaction with the Gal4-VP16 transcription factor (Prochasson et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: The QLC of SNF5 was required for rapid, efficient recruitment of SWI/SNF by the Gal4-VP16 activator.
source: In this context, we found that the QLC of SNF5 was required for rapid, efficient recruitment of SWI/SNF by the Gal4-VP16 activator, and that the pH of the buffer affected this recruitment (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro recruitment assay data presented in Figure 5F.

claim: The pH of the buffer affected recruitment of SWI/SNF by the Gal4-VP16 activator.
source: In this context, we found that the QLC of SNF5 was required for rapid, efficient recruitment of SWI/SNF by the Gal4-VP16 activator, and that the pH of the buffer affected this recruitment (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro recruitment assay data presented in Figure 5F.

claim: Within the physiological pH range (6.5–7.6), recruitment of SWI/SNF by Gal4-VP16 increased with pH.
source: Within the physiological pH range (6.5–7.6), recruitment and remodeling increased with pH.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro recruitment assay data presented in Figure 5F.

claim: SWI/SNF complexes deleted for the SNF5 QLC (containing ΔQsnf5p) had constitutively lower recruitment and were completely insensitive to pH changes over the physiological range.
source: SWI/SNF complexes deleted for the SNF5 QLC (containing ΔQsnf5p) had constitutively lower recruitment and were completely insensitive to pH changes over this same range (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro recruitment assay data presented in Figure 5G.

claim: SWI/SNF complexes containing HtoAsnf5p were even more defective than the ΔQsnf5 allele with respect to recruitment to the VP16 transcription factor.
source: SWI/SNF complexes containing HtoAsnf5p were even more defective that the ΔQsnf5 allele with respect to recruitment to the VP16 transcription factor (Figure 5H); this recruitment was barely above background levels at all pH values.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro recruitment assay data presented in Figure 5H.

claim: The SNF5 QLC can sense pH changes by modulating interactions between SWI/SNF and transcription factors.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the SNF5 QLC can sense pH changes by modulating interactions between SWI/SNF and transcription factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vitro recruitment assay data.

claim: The histidines within the SNF5 QLC must be present and deprotonated to enable interaction with VP16.
source: Furthermore, these results suggest that the histidines within the SNF5 QLC must be present and deprotonated to enable interaction with VP16.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pH-dependent recruitment data and the effect of histidine mutations.

claim: Charged amino acids have repeatedly been shown to govern the conformational behavior of disordered regions.
source: Charged amino acids have repeatedly been shown to govern the conformational behavior of disordered regions (Mao et al., 2010; Müller-Späth et al., 2010; Sorensen and Kjaergaard, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Protonation of the wild-type SNF5 QLC sequence (residues 71–120) led to a striking increase in the radius of gyration, driven by intramolecular electrostatic repulsions.
source: Protonation of the wild-type sequence led to a striking increase in the radius of gyration, driven by intramolecular electrostatic repulsions (Figure 6D, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by all-atom simulation data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: When 2/3 histidines in the SNF5 QLC (residues 71–120) were replaced with alanines, no change in radius of gyration upon protonation was observed.
source: In contrast, when 2/3 histidines were replaced with alanines, no such change was observed (Figure 6D, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by all-atom simulation data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: Protonation of the wild-type SNF5 QLC sequence (residues 71–120) led to a change in apparent scaling exponent (νapp) from 0.48 to 0.55.
source: For context, we also calculated an apparent scaling exponent (νapp), a dimensionless parameter that can also be used to quantify chain dimensions. This analysis showed that protonation of the wild-type sequence led to a change in νapp from 0.48 to 0.55, comparable to the magnitude of changes observed in previous studies of mutations that fundamentally altered intermolecular interactions in other low-complexity disordered regions (Martin et al., 2020; Sorensen and Kjaergaard, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by all-atom simulation data analysis.

claim: Small changes in sequence charge density can elicit a relatively large change in conformational behavior of the SNF5 QLC.
source: These results suggest that small changes in sequence charge density can elicit a relatively large change in conformational behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation data.

claim: An analogous (albeit less pronounced) effect of histidine protonation on radius of gyration was observed for the second QLC subregion (residues 195–233).
source: An analogous (albeit less pronounced) effect was observed for the second QLC subregion that we mutated (residues 195–233) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by all-atom simulation data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Charge-depleted disordered regions (such as QLCs) are poised to undergo pH-dependent conformational rearrangement.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that charge-depleted disordered regions (such as QLCs) are poised to undergo pH-dependent conformational rearrangement.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation data.

claim: The conformational expansion of the QLC sequence upon nucleocytoplasmic acidification may tune the propensity for SWI/SNF to interact with transcription factors.
source: This inference offers the beginnings of a mechanism for pH sensing by SWI/SNF: the conformational expansion of the QLC sequence upon nucleocytoplasmic acidification may tune the propensity for SWI/SNF to interact with transcription factors (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the simulation and experimental data.

claim: Previous studies have emphasized the inactivation of processes in response to cytosolic acidification.
source: Prior results have emphasized the inactivation of processes in response to cytosolic acidification (Joyner et al., 2016; Munder et al., 2016; Petrovska et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: This work establishes a positive regulatory role for nucleocytoplasmic pH changes during carbon starvation.
source: In this work, we found that transient acidification is required for activation of glucose-repressed genes. Therefore, our work establishes a positive regulatory role for nucleocytoplasmic pH changes during carbon starvation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Previous studies of intracellular state during glucose starvation based on population averages reported a simple decrease in pHi.
source: Previous studies of intracellular state during glucose starvation based on population averages reported a simple decrease in pHi (Orij et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Two coexisting subpopulations arose upon acute glucose starvation, one with pHi ~ 5.5 and a second at ~6.5.
source: In this work, we used single-cell measurements of both pHi and gene expression, and found that two coexisting subpopulations arose upon acute glucose starvation, one with pHi ~ 5.5 and a second at ~6.5.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell flow cytometry data.

claim: The population with pHi ~6.5 recovered to neutral pHi and then induced glucose-repressed genes, while the population with pHi ~5.5 remained dormant in an acidified state.
source: The latter population recovered to neutral pHi and then induced glucose-repressed genes, while the former remained dormant in an acidified state.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell flow cytometry data.

claim: It was previously shown that the protonation state of phosphatidic acid (PA) determines binding to the transcription factor Opi1, coupling membrane biogenesis and intracellular pH.
source: It was previously shown that the protonation state of phosphatidic acid (PA) determines binding to the transcription factor Opi1, coupling membrane biogenesis and intracellular pH (Young et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Histidines are good candidates for pH sensors as they can change protonation state over the recorded range of physiological pH fluctuations.
source: Histidines are good candidates for pH sensors as they can change protonation state over the recorded range of physiological pH fluctuations, and their pKa can be tuned substantially depending on local sequence context.
evidence: This is established knowledge about histidine chemistry.

claim: The pKa of histidine can be tuned substantially depending on local sequence context.
source: Histidines are good candidates for pH sensors as they can change protonation state over the recorded range of physiological pH fluctuations, and their pKa can be tuned substantially depending on local sequence context.
evidence: This is established knowledge about histidine chemistry.

claim: The intrinsic ATPase and nucleosome remodeling activities of SWI/SNF are robust to pH changes from 6.5 to 7.6.
source: Our in vitro assays showed that the intrinsic ATPase and nucleosome remodeling activities of SWI/SNF are robust to pH changes from 6.5 to 7.6.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro biochemical assay data.

claim: Recruitment of the SWI/SNF complex by a model transcription factor (GAL4-VP16) was pH-sensitive.
source: However, recruitment of the SWI/SNF complex by a model transcription factor (GAL4-VP16) was pH-sensitive, and this pH dependence was dependent on both the SNF5 QLC and the four central histidines within this domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro recruitment assay data.

claim: The pH dependence of SWI/SNF recruitment by GAL4-VP16 was dependent on both the SNF5 QLC and the four central histidines within this domain.
source: However, recruitment of the SWI/SNF complex by a model transcription factor (GAL4-VP16) was pH-sensitive, and this pH dependence was dependent on both the SNF5 QLC and the four central histidines within this domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro recruitment assay data.

claim: The recruitment of SWI/SNF by GAL4-VP16 was inhibited at pH 6.5.
source: In this case, the recruitment by GAL4-VP16 was inhibited at pH 6.5.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro recruitment assay data.

claim: Low pHi favors release of SWI/SNF from activators that it is bound to in glucose conditions.
source: We speculate that low pHi favors release of SWI/SNF from activators that it is bound to in glucose conditions, and then the subsequent partial recovery in pHi could allow it to bind to a different set of activators (e.g., ADR1 and CAT8), thus recruiting it to genes that are expressed during starvation.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed based on the data.

claim: Subsequent partial recovery in pHi could allow SWI/SNF to bind to a different set of activators (e.g., ADR1 and CAT8), thus recruiting it to genes that are expressed during starvation.
source: We speculate that low pHi favors release of SWI/SNF from activators that it is bound to in glucose conditions, and then the subsequent partial recovery in pHi could allow it to bind to a different set of activators (e.g., ADR1 and CAT8), thus recruiting it to genes that are expressed during starvation.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed based on the data.

claim: The model of pH-dependent SWI/SNF recruitment is consistent with the requirement for both acidification and subsequent neutralization for expression of ADH2.
source: This model is consistent with the requirement for both acidification and subsequent neutralization for expression of ADH2 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a statement of consistency between the model and the data.

claim: There are almost certainly additional pH-sensing elements of the transcriptional machinery that also take part in transcriptional reprogramming during carbon starvation.
source: In principle, the conformational dynamics of the SNF5 QLC could be distinct at all three stages (Figure 6E). There are almost certainly additional pH-sensing elements of the transcriptional machinery that also take part in this reprogramming; multiple candidates are present among the of transcription factors that were enriched in our RNA-seq experiments (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the complexity of the transcriptional response.

claim: Low-complexity sequences, including QLCs, tend to be intrinsically disordered and therefore highly solvent exposed.
source: Low-complexity sequences, including QLCs, tend to be intrinsically disordered and therefore highly solvent exposed.
evidence: This is established knowledge about low-complexity sequences.

claim: A recent large-scale study of intrinsically disordered sequences showed that their conformational behavior is inherently sensitive to changes in their solution environment.
source: A recent large-scale study of intrinsically disordered sequences showed that their conformational behavior is inherently sensitive to changes in their solution environment (Holehouse and Sukenik, 2020; Moses et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Upon acidification, histidines become positively charged, leading QLCs to adopt a more expanded state.
source: This provides a potential mechanism for pH sensing: upon acidification, histidines become positively charged, leading QLCs to adopt a more expanded state, perhaps revealing short linear interaction motifs (SLIMs), reducing the entropic cost of binding to interaction partners, preventing polar-mediated protein-protein interactions, or facilitating electrostatic-mediated contacts.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the simulation data.

claim: The enrichment of histidines in QLCs hints that pH-dependent conformational changes could be a general, widespread mechanism to regulate cell biology in response to pH changes.
source: The enrichment of histidines in QLCs hints that this could be a general, widespread mechanism to regulate cell biology in response to pH changes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the sequence analysis and experimental data.

claim: Glutamine-rich low-complexity sequences have been predominantly studied in the context of disease.
source: Glutamine-rich low-complexity sequences have been predominantly studied in the context of disease.
evidence: This is a statement about the focus of prior research.

claim: Nine neurodegenerative illnesses, including Huntington's disease, are thought to be caused by neurotoxic aggregation seeded by proteins that contain polyglutamines created by expansion of CAG trinucleotide repeats.
source: Nine neurodegenerative illnesses, including Huntington's disease, are thought to be caused by neurotoxic aggregation seeded by proteins that contain polyglutamines created by expansion of CAG trinucleotide repeats (Fan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Polyglutamines and glutamine-rich sequences are relatively abundant in Eukaryotic cells: more than 100 human proteins contain QLCs.
source: However, polyglutamines and glutamine-rich sequences are relatively abundant in Eukaryotic cells: more than 100 human proteins contain QLCs, and the Dictyostelium and Drosophilid phyla have QLCs in ~10% and ~5% of their proteins, respectively (Schaefer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: There is clear evidence of purifying selection to maintain polyQs in the Drosophilids.
source: Furthermore, there is clear evidence of purifying selection to maintain polyQs in the Drosophilids (Huntley and Clark, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: The prevalence and conservation of QLCs suggest an important biological function for these sequences.
source: This prevalence and conservation suggest an important biological function for these sequences.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary principles.

claim: Recent work in Ashbya gossypii has revealed a role for QLC-containing proteins in the organization of the cytoplasm through phase separation into liquid droplets to enable subcellular localization of signaling molecules.
source: Recent work in Ashbya gossypii has revealed a role for QLC-containing proteins in the organization of the cytoplasm through phase separation into liquid droplets to enable subcellular localization of signaling molecules (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Polyglutamine has been shown to drive self-association into a variety of higher-order assemblies, from fibrils to nanoscopic spheres to liquid droplets.
source: More generally, polyglutamine has been shown to drive self-association into a variety of higher-order assemblies, from fibrils to nanoscopic spheres to liquid droplets (Crick et al., 2013; Peskett et al., 2018; Posey et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: QLCs may offer a general mechanism to drive protein-protein interactions.
source: Taken together, these results imply that QLCs may offer a general mechanism to drive protein-protein interactions.

claim: The current model is that the SNF5 QLC partakes in heterotypic protein interactions that are modulated by protonation of histidines when the cell interior acidifies.
